script.opening: "I twisted my knee playing football a few days ago — my foot was planted and I turned. It swelled up that evening, and now it clicks and catches, gives way, and a couple of times it’s locked so I literally couldn’t straighten it. What’s going on — do I need a scan?"

facts.text: Five days ago, Sunday league. Right foot planted, turned to the left. Sharp pain on the inner side of the knee. No pop he remembers. Played on for 5 minutes then came off. Swelling came up "by the evening", not straight away.

Went to the urgent treatment centre that night. If asked what they found: "They said there was fluid in the knee and it was tender on the inside line, but I could bend it past a right angle and walk, and the kneecap wasn’t tender, so no X-ray." He has the discharge letter.

Clicks and catches on the inside. Gave way twice going downstairs. Twice it "locked": stuck bent for a minute and he couldn’t straighten it, then it clunked and freed. Can fully straighten it now, just sore. Can walk with a limp.
No numbness or tingling in the foot, calf not swollen or tender, no fever, knee not hot or red. No previous knee injuries.
No medicines except ibuprofen since the injury. No asthma, no stomach problems, no allergies. Works as a plumber — kneeling and stairs all day. Self-employed. Lives with girlfriend.
Frustrated, keen to get back to football and work. Ask "So no scan?" if a scan isn’t mentioned, and "So I will need an operation?" if referral is suggested. Accept a plan that gets you seen quickly.

ice.concerns: "That I’ll need an operation and miss the season. And I don’t trust it now." Worried about losing income as a self-employed plumber.

cues: "It’s locked so I couldn’t straighten it" — true locking needs urgent referral.
"They didn’t X-ray it" (if asked) — Ottawa knee rules were applied.
"I’m self-employed and kneel all day" — work impact and fit note.

checkpoints.text: Recognises the MENISCAL pattern (twisting injury, effusion over hours, joint-line tenderness, mechanical symptoms — clicking/catching/giving way/locking; McMurray supportive but not reliable enough to exclude)
Applies the OTTAWA KNEE RULES to decide on X-ray (age ≥55, isolated patellar/fibular-head tenderness, inability to flex 90°, inability to weight-bear 4 steps) to exclude fracture

Recognises the TRUE LOCKED KNEE (cannot fully extend — bucket-handle tear) and acute ACL injury (immediate haemarthrosis, pop, instability) as needing urgent orthopaedic/MRI assessment (BASK 2019; same day if locked now), and asks about fever/a hot joint to exclude septic arthritis
Manages stable, non-locking meniscal injuries initially conservatively (RICE, analgesia, physiotherapy/quadriceps rehab, activity modification), starting these while he awaits MRI

Arranges MRI and ORTHOPAEDIC referral for a true locked knee or true locking in a young person (urgent, BASK 2019), persistent mechanical symptoms, suspected ACL/ligament injury, or failed conservative management — not imaging reflexively
Explains the diagnosis and imaging/referral reasoning, addresses his concern about a scan, and checks understanding
Acknowledges the impact on his sport and his wish to get back to football, and agrees a shared rehab plan and the point at which they would escalate to imaging

Safety-nets and follows up: same-day A&E for a knee locked now/inability to weight-bear/hot very swollen knee, review for continued giving way, conservative plan with physio, and MRI/orthopaedics where indicated

worked.txt: "A twisting injury with the knee swelling up over a few hours, then clicking, catching and locking, points to a cartilage (meniscus) tear. The locking — not being able to straighten it — is an important feature."

"Let me check a few things that tell me whether you need an X-ray to rule out a fracture — can you bend it to 90 degrees, walk four steps, any tenderness on the kneecap or the side of the knee? … That guides imaging."

"Did it swell instantly with a pop, and does it give way? Immediate swelling and instability can mean a ligament (ACL) injury, and a knee that truly locks needs the orthopaedic team and a scan more urgently."

"Because your knee has genuinely locked, I’ll arrange an MRI and a knee specialist — in someone your age a displaced tear may be repairable, and that works best early. Meanwhile: rest from football and twisting, ice, keep it raised, painkillers and — importantly — physiotherapy to strengthen the thigh muscles and restore movement."

"The scan will show what’s torn and whether repair would help — some tears settle with physiotherapy, some need a keyhole operation, and the giving way means the ligaments need checking too. Any fever, or has the knee gone hot and red?"
"Go to A&E the same day if it locks and won’t unlock, you can’t put weight on it, or it becomes hot and very swollen. Otherwise I’ll send the referral today, start physio, and review in two weeks."

f.learning: A MENISCAL TEAR is suggested by a TWISTING injury on a planted/loaded knee, an EFFUSION developing over hours (rather than immediately), JOINT-LINE tenderness, and MECHANICAL symptoms — clicking, catching, giving way and LOCKING — with McMurray’s test able to support but not reliably exclude the diagnosis. Apply the OTTAWA KNEE RULES (Stiell 1996–1997, international) to decide on X-ray (to exclude fracture): image if age ≥55, isolated patellar tenderness, fibular-head tenderness, inability to flex to 90°, or inability to weight-bear for 4 steps (immediately and in clinic). Recognise the more urgent presentations: a TRUE LOCKED KNEE or true locking episodes in a young person (unable to fully extend, often a displaced bucket-handle meniscal tear blocking the joint) need urgent MRI and orthopaedic review because early repair may be possible (BASK 2019), with same-day assessment if locked now, and an acute ACL injury — immediate haemarthrosis (rapid swelling), an audible "pop" and instability/giving way — warrants orthopaedic/MRI assessment; distinguish a genuinely locked knee from pain-limited pseudo-locking. Screen for septic arthritis (fever, hot joint). Manage stable, non-locking meniscal injuries initially conservatively (RICE, analgesia, physiotherapy with quadriceps strengthening and range of motion, activity modification), as many small/degenerate tears settle (NICE NG226 for degenerative knees), and arrange MRI and orthopaedic referral for a true locked knee (urgent), persistent significant mechanical symptoms, suspected ACL/ligament injury, or failure of conservative management — with arthroscopy in selected cases. Safety-net for locking that won’t unlock, inability to weight-bear, or instability, or a hot very swollen knee.

knowledge.guideline: [1] Ottawa knee rules (Stiell et al., JAMA 1996–1997) (international) · [2] BASK Meniscal Working Group: arthroscopic meniscal surgery treatment guideline and consensus statement (Bone Joint J 2019) · [3] ESSKA meniscus consensus (2016–2017) (international) · [4] NICE NG226 (osteoarthritis in over 16s, 2022) · [5] MHRA Drug Safety Update June 2015 (high-dose ibuprofen)
knowledge.summary: A twisting injury on a planted foot, swelling that builds over hours, joint-line tenderness and mechanical symptoms suggest a meniscal tear. Use the Ottawa knee rules to decide whether an X-ray is needed. A knee that truly locks, or has locked, in a young person points to a displaced tear and needs MRI and orthopaedic review; a knee locked now needs same-day assessment. Swelling within an hour or two with a pop and giving way suggests an ACL tear. Stable, non-locking tears can start with physiotherapy.

points.t: Twisting on a loaded knee, swelling developing over several hours rather than at once, pain on the joint line, and clicking, catching, giving way or locking. McMurray’s test can support the diagnosis but is not reliable enough to exclude it.

X-ray after acute knee injury if any of: age 55 or over, isolated tenderness of the patella, tenderness of the fibular head, unable to flex to 90°, or unable to bear weight for four steps both immediately and in the clinic [1]. If none apply, a fracture is unlikely and an X-ray is not needed.

True locking is a mechanical block to full extension, often from a displaced bucket-handle tear. Pseudo-locking is pain or swelling limiting movement. BASK 2019 [2] advises urgent MRI and orthopaedic review for a locked knee, because a displaced tear may be repairable if treated early. A knee that is locked now needs same-day assessment.

A pop with swelling within an hour or two (haemarthrosis) and a feeling of the knee shifting suggest an anterior cruciate ligament tear, which often coexists with a meniscal tear. Consider collateral ligament injury, patellar dislocation and fracture.

In a young person with an acute traumatic tear and mechanical symptoms, early MRI and specialist review are appropriate because repair preserves the meniscus [2][3]. Degenerative tears in older people are usually treated with exercise, and arthroscopic washout or debridement is not offered for osteoarthritis unless the knee is truly locking (NICE NG226 [4]).

Relative rest, ice and elevation, crutches if weight-bearing is painful, paracetamol or an NSAID at the lowest effective dose (BNF; MHRA June 2015 [5]), and early quadriceps and range-of-movement exercises. Avoid pivoting sport until assessed.
Same-day assessment if the knee locks and will not unlock, he cannot bear weight, or the knee becomes hot and very swollen. Review if giving way continues.

model.text: Hello Mr Okonkwo, I’m Dr Hughes. What’s brought you in?

I twisted my knee playing football a few days ago. My foot was planted and I turned. It swelled up that evening, and now it clicks and catches, gives way, and a couple of times it’s locked so I literally couldn’t straighten it. What’s going on? Do I need a scan?

That sounds like a proper injury. I’ll ask about exactly what happened, go through the examination findings in your notes and look at the knee on the camera, and then we’ll decide about a scan together. Okay?
Yes.
When you twisted it, did you hear or feel a pop, and could you carry on playing?
I don’t really remember a pop. It just hurt.
Did it swell straight away, within an hour or so, or later that evening?
model.why: Timing of effusion: ACL versus meniscus

model.text: Later, by the evening it was puffy.
Tell me about the locking. When it happened, could you get it straight again, and how?
It got stuck bent for a bit, then it went back.
Can you straighten it fully right now, and could you walk on it after the injury and today?
I can straighten it now, it’s just sore. I can walk on it.
When it gives way, does it feel like the knee shifts out of place?
It just goes sometimes.
Have you had any fever, or has the knee gone hot and red?
No.
How is this affecting you, at work and with football?
Football’s a big part of my life. I want to know how long I’m out.
What do you think you’ve done?
Cartilage, maybe. A mate had that.
What’s worrying you most?
That I’ll need an operation and miss the season. And I don’t trust it now.

Your notes have the examination from your earlier appointment — swelling, joint-line tenderness, the kneecap and top of the shin bone, ligaments and range of movement. Can you show me both knees on the camera, bend and straighten them, and walk a few steps for me?
model.why: Uses the recorded knee examination (Ottawa criteria, ligament tests) and video observation of movement and gait

model.text: Okay.

The twist on a planted foot, swelling by the evening, and then catching and locking point to a tear of the meniscus, the cartilage cushion in the knee. By the rules we use, you don’t need an X-ray for a fracture if you can bend it past a right angle, walk four steps and have no tenderness on the kneecap or the top of the outer shin bone.
model.why: Names the likely diagnosis and applies the Ottawa rules

model.text: So no scan?

Not an X-ray, but I do think you need an MRI and a knee specialist. When a knee genuinely locks, a torn piece may be flipping into the joint. In someone your age, the surgeons may be able to repair it, and that works best if it’s done early. The giving way also needs the ligaments checked.
model.why: MRI and orthopaedic referral for true locking in a young traumatic tear

model.text: So I will need an operation?

Not necessarily. The scan will show what’s torn and whether repair would help. Some tears settle with physiotherapy. Either way, getting the right answer early gives your knee the best chance long term.
model.why: Honest, balanced answer to his fear

model.text: Okay. What do I do meanwhile?

Rest it from football and twisting, use ice and keep it raised, and take paracetamol or ibuprofen if you can take it. Keep it moving with gentle straightening and thigh-muscle exercises. I’ll also refer you to physio. Would that work for you?
Yes.

If it locks and won’t come free, you can’t put weight on it, or it becomes hot and very swollen, go to A&E the same day. Otherwise I’ll send the referral today and we’ll review in two weeks. Can you tell me the plan?
MRI and knee specialist, physio, no football, ice and painkillers. A&E if it locks and stays stuck or I can’t walk.
That’s it.

social.t: Football is central to his life. A clear plan and timeline help him accept time out now to protect the knee long term.
Explore his job. If it involves standing, climbing or lifting, he may need adjustments or a fit note while waiting for assessment.

legal.t: He should drive only if he can control the car safely, including an emergency stop. Notification to the DVLA is needed only if a limb problem stops him driving for more than three months (GOV.UK).

professional.t: Using decision rules and clinical features for imaging avoids unnecessary radiation while making sure the right scan is done (GMC Good medical practice).

community.t: MSK physiotherapy, self-referral where available; club physio or sports injury clinics for return-to-sport rehabilitation.

playbook.diagnosis: Probable acute traumatic meniscal tear with true locking episodes and giving way; ACL injury to be excluded. No Ottawa criteria for X-ray.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “You’ve probably torn the cartilage cushion inside the knee. A loose piece can catch and lock the knee, which is why it gets stuck.”

management.reflectIce: “You wanted to know about a scan. You don’t need an X-ray, but the locking means an MRI and a knee specialist are the right next step.”
management.psychosocial: Honest discussion of surgery; timeline for sport; work adjustments if needed.
sharedPlan: MRI and orthopaedic referral for true locking
Physiotherapy: quadriceps and range of movement

safetyNet: Locked and will not free, or unable to weight-bear: A&E the same day

pitfalls.intro: This station tests whether you image the right thing for the right reason, and spot the locking that changes the plan.

items.fail: Ordering an X-ray to look for a cartilage tear.
items.why: X-rays do not show the meniscus; Ottawa rules decide X-ray.
items.fix: Apply the Ottawa rules and explain MRI is the test for the meniscus.

items.fail: Treating a truly locking knee as a sprain.
items.why: A displaced tear may be repairable only if seen early.

items.fail: Not asking about swelling timing and giving way.
items.why: Rapid swelling and instability suggest an ACL tear.
items.fix: Ask about a pop, swelling within hours and instability; test ligaments.

items.why: A hot swollen knee with fever is an emergency.
items.fix: Ask about fever and a hot joint.

items.why: He fears surgery; certainty either way is misleading.
items.fix: Explain the scan will guide it.

items.fail: No safety net for a stuck knee.
items.why: A knee locked now needs same-day care.
items.fix: Give clear A&E triggers and a review date.

wordPics.fail: Orders an X-ray for everyone or no imaging at all; misses the true locking; ‘rest and it will settle’.
wordPics.pass: Recognises a meniscal tear, applies the Ottawa rules, refers for MRI and orthopaedics because of locking and safety-nets.
wordPics.exc: All of that, plus: distinguishes true from pseudo-locking, considers ACL injury, explains why early review matters for repair in a young person, and handles his fear of surgery honestly.

avoid.dont: “Let’s X-ray it to see the cartilage.”
avoid.instead: “An X-ray shows bone, and you don’t meet the rules for one. An MRI shows the cartilage.”
avoid.why: X-rays do not show meniscal tears; the Ottawa rules guide X-ray use.

avoid.instead: “The locking tells me something may be caught in the joint, so a specialist should see it.”
avoid.why: True locking suggests a displaced tear needing early review.

avoid.instead: “The scan will show whether repair would help.”
avoid.why: Premature certainty increases anxiety and may be wrong.

Hot, red, very swollen knee or fever: septic arthritis
Swelling within an hour or two with a pop: haemarthrosis, likely ACL
psychosocial: Football is a big part of his life
Fear of surgery and missing the season
Loss of trust in the knee
ice: Concern: surgery and time out of sport

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Probable acute traumatic meniscal tear with true locking episodes and giving way; ACL injury to be excluded. No Ottawa criteria for X-ray.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “You’ve probably torn the cartilage cushion inside the knee. A loose piece can catch and lock the knee, which is why it gets stuck.”

management.reflectIce: “You wanted to know about a scan. You don’t need an X-ray, but the locking means an MRI and a knee specialist are the right next step.”
management.psychosocial: Honest discussion of surgery; timeline for sport; work adjustments if needed.
sharedPlan: MRI and orthopaedic referral for true locking
Physiotherapy: quadriceps and range of movement
Rest from pivoting sport; ice, elevation
Paracetamol or ibuprofen if suitable, dose per BNF
safetyNet: Locked and will not free, or unable to weight-bear: A&E the same day
Hot, very swollen knee or fever: same day

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station tests whether you image the right thing for the right reason, and spot the locking that changes the plan.

items.fail: Ordering an X-ray to look for a cartilage tear.
items.why: X-rays do not show the meniscus; Ottawa rules decide X-ray.
items.fix: Apply the Ottawa rules and explain MRI is the test for the meniscus.

items.fail: Treating a truly locking knee as a sprain.
items.why: A displaced tear may be repairable only if seen early.

items.fail: Not asking about swelling timing and giving way.
items.why: Rapid swelling and instability suggest an ACL tear.
items.fix: Ask about a pop, swelling within hours and instability; test ligaments.

items.why: A hot swollen knee with fever is an emergency.
items.fix: Ask about fever and a hot joint.

items.why: He fears surgery; certainty either way is misleading.
items.fix: Explain the scan will guide it.

items.fail: No safety net for a stuck knee.
items.why: A knee locked now needs same-day care.
items.fix: Give clear A&E triggers and a review date.
